title: Partnership Arithmetic
tagline: Year 2 — Sharing profit and loss by capital and time

introduction.overview: In a partnership two or more people invest money in a business and share the profit or loss. The fair share of each partner is proportional to the amount of money they put in and the time for which it stays invested. The key quantity is therefore capital × time, and the profit is divided in the ratio of these products.
introduction.placementRelevance: Partnership questions are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds. They are ratio problems in a business setting, usually with two or three partners and one twist such as a late entry, a withdrawal or a salary for a working partner.
introduction.realWorldContext: Joint ventures, startup co-founders and shared investments all divide returns using capital and time.

learningObjectives: Divide profit and loss in the ratio of capital × time
Handle partners who join or leave during the year
Handle working partners who receive a salary or a commission
Work with fractions and percentages of capital
Find the total profit from a known share

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: To divide N in the ratio a : b : c, one part = N ÷ (a + b + c). Compare capital × time products by simplifying their ratio.

coreDefinitions: Partnership: an arrangement in which two or more persons invest in a business and share the result.
Capital: the money invested. Period: the time for which the capital stays in the business.
Sleeping (silent) partner: invests money but does not work. Working partner: manages the business and may receive a salary or commission.
Profit-sharing ratio: ratio of (capital × time) of the partners.
Loss is shared in the same ratio as profit.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: A rupee kept for 12 months earns twice as much as a rupee kept for 6 months. So the natural unit is the "rupee-month". Each partner's share equals their rupee-months divided by everyone's total rupee-months.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Write each partner's investment as a row of "capital × months". Multiply, simplify the products as a ratio, and share the profit in that ratio.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Equal time
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: If all capital stays the same time, time cancels.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Equal capital
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: If capitals are equal, the ratio of times.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Salary or commission
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Deduct the salary or commission first, then share the remaining profit by the ratio
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: The working partner receives it in addition to the share.

mainNarrative: Start by writing, for each partner, the capital and the number of months. Convert partners who join later to the number of months they actually invest. If B joins after 3 months in a 12-month year, B's time is 9 months.

Multiply capital by time for each partner and write the products as a ratio. Simplify by common factors. In the example where A invests ₹4,500 for 12 months, B ₹6,000 for 9 months and C ₹9,000 for 6 months, the products are 54,000, 54,000 and 54,000, so profit is shared equally.
If a partner changes the capital during the year, split the year into periods. A starts with ₹5,000, adds ₹1,000 after 6 months: 5000 × 6 + 6000 × 6 = 66,000.

Working partners: subtract the salary or commission from the profit first. If the manager gets 10% of profit and profit is ₹11,000, ₹1,100 goes to the manager. Share the remaining ₹9,900 in the capital ratio and add the salary to the manager's share.
If only one partner's share is known, the total profit is found by proportion: if A's share is 5 parts of 8 and equals ₹3,000, one part is ₹600 and the total is ₹4,800.

deepDiveAspects.title: Why capital × time
deepDiveAspects.content: Profit is the return on use of money. Doubling the capital or doubling the time doubles the return, so both multiply.

deepDiveAspects.title: Losses
deepDiveAspects.content: Loss is shared in the same ratio as profit. The salary of a working partner does not apply if there is a loss unless stated.

solvedExamples.title: Different capitals and times
solvedExamples.question: A invests ₹4,000 for 12 months and B invests ₹6,000 for 8 months. The profit is ₹9,600. Find each share.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Larger capital for a shorter time gives the same rupee-months.

solvedExamples.title: Partner joins late
solvedExamples.question: A starts a business with ₹3,500. After 5 months B joins with ₹6,000. At the end of the year the profit is ₹8,400. Find B's share.

solvedExamples.title: Working partner with commission
solvedExamples.question: A and B invest ₹6,000 and ₹9,000. A is the manager and gets 10% of the profit for managing, and the rest is shared in the ratio of capitals. The profit is ₹11,000. Find B's share.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: B receives only the capital share; the commission goes to A.

shortcutMethods.title: Rupee-month table

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Work out each partner's return separately.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Fill a one-line table of capital × months, simplify the ratio and divide the profit once.

rulesForApplication: Equal time → capital ratio; equal capital → time ratio.
Deduct salary or commission before sharing.
Check that the shares add up to the profit.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Using the joining month as the period.

commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Pay the salary first to the working partner.
Split the year at the change.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Shares must add to the profit and follow the ratio order; discard options that do not.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Do capital × time on paper; do not compute mentally for three partners.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Partnership questions often reuse ratio tricks like matching common terms.

summaryBullets: Equal time → capitals; equal capital → times.
Loss shares follow the same ratio.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I compute capital × time for each partner?
Can I handle a partner who joins late?
Can I deduct a manager's commission?
